text: A guest book that knows who is coming. The lantern is lit.
picture: The Storyteller stands in a dark, misty hollow, a glowing red lantern held low in his hand. His face is solemn, the mist curling around his boots. In the faint red light, far behind him, the dark outline of a lonely roadside motel, foggy and indistinct, with one small window lit.

text: I work the night desk at the Wayside Motel, out on Route 9, where the road runs between two towns that don't talk to each other.
picture: A wide, establishing shot of the Wayside Motel at night: a single-storey, run-down building with a long row of identical doors. Fog blankets the scene, and a single two-lane road is visible, empty and stretching into darkness. Only one window in the front office is lit.

text: Twelve rooms. Most nights, nobody comes.
picture: A shot along the motel's deserted exterior walkway, looking at the row of dark, identical doors under long shadows cast by a lone overhead light. Fog drifts across the empty concrete. The single lit office window glows faintly in the background.

text: The guest book sits open on the counter. The owner, Mr. Pell, likes ink. He says a name in ink is a promise.
picture: A close-up insert of the old, worn wooden motel counter. An open leather guest book lies under the warm, focused glow of a single desk lamp. A fountain pen rests beside it. The page shows columns of faded, unreadable handwriting.

text: Every morning, when I hand over the keys, there's a new line in it. Room six. Signed at two fourteen a. m. A different name every night.
picture: June stands at the counter in cold, early morning light, looking weary. One hand holds a heavy ring of motel keys. Her other index finger rests just below a single, stark line of dark blood-red ink in the open guest book. The fresh writing is an unreadable blur.

text: Room six has been boarded up since before I was hired.
picture: Outside under a dim, yellow bulb, a single motel door is criss-crossed with weathered grey wooden planks nailed shut. The brass number 6 hangs crookedly. A deep, unnatural fog presses closely against the door. The rest of the walkway is in heavy shadow.

text: The first week, I blamed the day staff. The second week, I stopped blaming anyone. I started watching.
picture: June sits rigid at the front desk, both hands clutching her phone. The open guest book lies before her, its red ink hidden. Blackness fills the window behind her. Her face is pale, alert, and hollow with fatigue.

text: Last night, at two thirteen, the lights in the parking lot flickered.
picture: A wide view of the motel office from the inside. June is a small, tense figure at the desk. Outside the window, the parking lot's sodium lights strobe and gutter, throwing sickly orange pulses across the dark room.

text: At two fourteen, the pen moved.
picture: An extreme close insert on the surface of the guest book. A dark wood fountain pen lies at a slight, unnatural angle, as if nudged. The desk lamp light is dim and unsteady, casting long, trembling shadows. No hand is seen.

text: Not much. Just a roll. Like someone had brushed it with a sleeve.
picture: Close on June's face. It's lit only by the cold blue glow of her phone screen. Her eyes are wide, staring fixedly at the phone, refusing to look down. Her jaw is tight with dread.

text: I didn't look at the book. I looked at the camera. On the screen, I was sitting at the desk.
picture: June's phone screen in a low-angle shot. On the screen is a grainy black-and-white security feed view. It shows the back of June's head as she sits at the desk. The rest of the dim office stretches out behind her.

text: And behind me, close enough to breathe on my neck, a
picture: The same phone screen, viewed from behind June's shoulder. The grainy CCTV image shows the back of her head and, directly behind her, the top of a tall, thin, hooded figure in a dark, dripping raincoat. It is bent slightly forward.

text: man in a wet raincoat was leaning over my shoulder to write.
picture: A wide 'CCTV' view from the high corner of the office. June sits at the desk. Directly behind her, the tall, skeletal figure in the dripping dark raincoat bends over her shoulder, its hooded face aimed down at the guest book, one pale hand reaching for the pen.

text: I didn't turn around. I couldn't.
picture: A side profile of June, rigidly facing forward at the desk, her neck muscles taut. The view includes the raincoated figure's shadow stretching towards her from behind, cast by the flickering light. Her wide eyes reflect the CCTV screen in front of her.

text: When the lights came back, the office was empty.
picture: Wide shot of the empty motel office, dim overhead light glowing on the counter, the guest book open, a dark puddle of liquid beside it, shadows pooling in the corners.
sound: a faint, buzzing hum from the lights

text: The book was open. The ink was still wet. Room six.
picture: Extreme close-up on the guest book page. 'June Marsh, Room 6' is written in glistening red ink, a fresh bead of liquid about to drip from the final letter. A water stain darkens the paper.

text: Two fourteen a. m. And the name was mine.
picture: June stands frozen behind the counter, her hand hovering over the open guest book, her face pale in the low light as she stares at the fresh red writing.

text: Mr. Pell came in at six. He read the line very quietly.
picture: Mr. Pell stands just inside the open office door, morning light from outside framing him. He holds his reading glasses, looking down at the guest book on the counter with a quiet, grim expression.

text: Then he took a key off the hook. A key I had never seen.
picture: Mr. Pell's old, wrinkled hand holds up a tarnished brass key on a frayed red tag against the key rack, which is otherwise filled with ordinary silver keys.
sound: the soft jingle of a key

text: "It's always the one at the desk," he said. "Your room's ready."
picture: Mr. Pell behind the counter, his mouth slightly open as he speaks softly. He holds up the tarnished key, his kind, weary face and sad eyes looking directly at June across the counter.

text: The Wayside Motel is still open. The night desk is always staffed. And if you sign the book, check the name above yours.
picture: The Storyteller, lit only by the red glow of his lowered lantern, stands in the misty hollow. Far behind him through the fog, the dark row of motel doors stretches into the distance.
